newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ long bonds set to outperform, short end pinched.
newsitem.headline: NZ long bonds set to outperform, short end pinched.

text.p: New Zealand long bonds, free of the many troubles plaguing the short end of the yield curve, should outperform the dollar bloc, analysts said on Thursday.
A government auction of a new July 2009 benchmark saw the first NZ$150 million tranche snapped up greedily, and dealers expect offshore investing interest to continue.

They said that, in theory, the 2009 bond should have yielded around 6.92 percent at tender, eight basis points above the 11/06 maturity. However, the exceptional demand narrowed that spread right down and the bonds yielded 6.825 percent.

The auction attracted 55 bids worth NZ$976 million, and just three were accepted. Analysts said the aggressive pricing and strong interest in the bond market confirmed that supply was tight and opened the door for further substantial gains.
"For the longer term investor these are fantastic rates," said ANZ Bank's manager of bond trading Rowan Addison.
Dealers were now seen rubbing their hands in anticipation of next week's June quarter inflation data, where the risks are all expected to be on the downside.

On average, 11 economists polled by Reuters expect quarterly core inflation of 0.33 percent. They see the annual rate dropping from 1.97 percent to 1.5 percent, in the middle of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's (RBNZ) 0-3 percent target band.
UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said the Consumers Price Index data would point to the continuing good value of New Zealand's long end.
"I would expect to see the New Zealand long bonds starting to outperform the rest of the dollar bloc over the course of the next few weeks," he said.
"We're looking at very subdued economic growth and we're looking at inflation which will not only come down but will continue to come down through the next six to nine months."

However, while the long bonds revel in their good fortunes the short end of the yield curve is struggling. The Reserve Bank recently ticked markets off for easing conditions too far, and bills have had to take up the slack of a falling currency.

Key 90-day bank bill rates have risen to 7.36 percent from 7.12 percent at the start of the week, as the kiwi dollar's Trade-Weighted Index dropped to just below 66.0 from 66.41. The TWI has not been that low since October last year.
A high overnight cash rate, currently at 7.75 percent, has also undermined the short end by making it expensive to hold physical bills.
"It's bizarre that we have a yield curve shaped this way with the economy in the situation it is," a Wellington bonds manager said.
"The question is, how far do interest rates have to go to attract interest in the kiwi?"
ANZ's Addison said the fact that monetary conditions were 64 basis points easier than the RBNZ's assumed level showed the market felt the current high short rates were unjustifiable.
The RBNZ has said it would tolerate conditions 50 basis points either side of its assumptions.
Addison said a bullish inflation result on Tuesday could see a stand-off between the market and the central bank.
"You could suddenly see the MCI jump up to 80 points (too loose). I think you probably will, in fact. And then what's the Reserve Bank going to do?
"It will be a matter of watch this space, because the kiwi is not going to get bought on a good CPI result, but bill rates will and cash will probably start to come down," he said.
-- Wellington newsroom (64 4) 473 4746
